# Nature follows simple mathematical laws (`mathematical_laws_of_nature`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by measurement_quantification, geometry_proof, falling_bodies
- Core idea: Regularities in nature can be written as exact relations between measured quantities, and such relations predict cases never yet observed. Start with ones anyone can check: a string stopped at half its length sounds the octave, at two thirds the fifth; a lever balances when weight times distance is equal on both sides; a pendulum four times as long takes twice as long to swing; a ball rolling down a groove covers distances as 1, 4, 9, 16 in equal times. The trick that makes this work is idealisation: strip away friction and air, find the simple law, then add the disturbances back as corrections. The claim is not that qualities and purposes are unreal, only that asking 'how much' gives answers that can be tested and built upon.
- Pitfalls:
  - Asserting that the laws are exact for real objects; they hold for idealised cases and must be corrected for friction, air and error
  - Quoting formulas (F = ma, E = mc²) without units, definitions or a way to check them, which is indistinguishable from numerology
  - Forgetting that mathematical astronomy already existed (Babylon, Ptolemy, Kerala, China); the new claim is that earthly physics is mathematical too
  - Numerology and Pythagorean mysticism are the nearest familiar idea; listeners will hear cosmic harmony, not measurement
- History: mesopotamia: c. 450–50 BC – arithmetical schemes predict lunar and planetary positions; greece: c. 500 BC – Pythagorean string ratios; c. 250 BC Archimedes' laws of the lever and of floating bodies; c. 150 AD Ptolemy; china: Han period – numerical harmonics of pitch pipes and calendar astronomy; little attempt to mathematise terrestrial motion; india: 499 – Aryabhata's computational astronomy; 14th–16th c. Kerala school; islamic: c. 1021 – Ibn al-Haytham combines geometry and experiment in optics; c. 1020s al-Biruni; 1121 al-Khazini on hydrostatics; europe: c. 1335 – Merton 'calculators' prove the mean-speed theorem; c. 1350 Oresme graphs changing quantities; 1623 Galileo: the book of nature is written in mathematics; 1638 law of fall; 1687 Newton's Principia
- Read:
  - Galileo Galilei, Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (1638)
  - E. J. Dijksterhuis, The Mechanization of the World Picture (1961)
  - Eugene P. Wigner, The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences (1960)
